events.description: Babbage completes the full design of the Analytical Engine
Prime Minister Peel reverses course and funds construction
Joseph Clement standardises the engine’s gears and screw threads
Ada Lovelace publishes Note G, the first program
The Engine computes Bernoulli numbers before the Royal Society
The Admiralty orders engines to compute navigation tables
Lloyd’s opens an actuarial engine room for the insurance market
The Bank of England moves its ledgers onto engines
Lovelace founds the School of Engine Programming in London
The 1851 census is tabulated entirely by engine
The Great Exhibition’s centrepiece is a working engine hall
Engines in London and Manchester exchange results by telegraph
Prussia buys three engines for its General Staff
Ten thousand clerks protest at Westminster against the engines
Manchester clerks hold a demonstration in solidarity
Parliament debates engine licensing legislation
Parliament passes the Engine Licensing Act
Moltke uses engine-planned railway timetables to mobilise
Britain and Prussia begin an engine arms race

events.description: The waters rise; the survivors crown the first salt-king on Hollow Isle
The salt-kings fix the weight of the salt coin
The tide-priests begin the Reckoning, counting years from the Rising
The glassmakers of Ambry are forbidden to trade without the king's salt
The salt-kings tax the tide-priests' shrines
The priests close the harbours; the Tide War begins
The glassmakers of Ambry side with the priests
The last salt-king drowns at the Siege of Hollow Isle
The Glass Republic is proclaimed in Ambry

arcs.name: The Age of Salt
arcs.description: From the Rising to the closing of the harbours: the salt-kings rule Hollow Isle.

arcs.name: The Tide War
arcs.description: The tide-priests against the salt-kings, and the glassmakers who decided it.

arcs.name: The Glass Republic
arcs.description: Ambry's republic of glassmakers, after the last salt-king.

relationships.evidence: The salt-kings' crown rested on salt.
A fixed coin made the shrines' salt worth taxing.
Keeping the count of years had made the shrines rich and powerful.
The Reckoning gave the priests authority over the harbours' tides.
The priests answered the tax by closing the harbours.
Thirty years of the salt ban had made the glassmakers enemies of the crown.
The war gave the glassmakers their chance.
Ambry's fleet closed the siege.
With no king left, Ambry proclaimed a republic.
